```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
options(mc.cores = 2)
```

bmbeR walks a regression model through the stages of a Bayesian workflow
(Gelman et al., 2020) and treats the prior as part of the model at every
stage:

1. Specify priors on the scale of the data.
2. Check what they imply *before* seeing the outcome (prior predictive check).
3. Fit the model and verify the computation (R-hat, effective sample size,
   divergences, E-BFMI).
4. Quantify how much the prior influenced the result (power-scaling sensitivity).
5. Evaluate predictions with proper scoring rules.
6. Report each step in a checklist aligned with the Bayesian Analysis
   Reporting Guidelines (Kruschke, 2021).

Models are fitted with [rstanarm](https://mc-stan.org/rstanarm/), so every
result is an ordinary `stanreg` object that works with the rest of the Stan
ecosystem.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(bmbeR)
data(kidiq, package = "rstanarm")
head(kidiq)
```

The `kidiq` data (Gelman & Hill, 2007) record the test scores of 434 children
together with their mothers' IQ and whether the mother finished high school.
We hold out a test set to evaluate predictions at the end.

```{r}
set.seed(42)
test_rows <- sample(nrow(kidiq), 100)
train <- kidiq[-test_rows, ]
test  <- kidiq[test_rows, ]
```

## 1. Specify priors

Priors only make sense relative to the units of the data. Children's test
scores are on an IQ-like scale (mean about 100, SD about 15), so:

* the **intercept** is the expected score of a child whose mother has average
  IQ and schooling (rstanarm puts the intercept prior at the predictor means,
  so you don't have to centre the predictors yourself): `normal(100, 20)`;
* a one-point increase in the mother's IQ is unlikely to change the child's
  score by more than about two points: `normal(0, 1)` for `mom_iq`;
* finishing high school might plausibly shift scores by up to about 20 points:
  `normal(0, 10)` for `mom_hs`;
* the residual SD is probably of the order of 15 points: `exponential(1/15)`.

```{r}
priors <- prior_config(
  intercept = prior_spec("normal", location = 100, scale = 20),
  slope     = prior_spec("normal", location = 0, scale = c(1, 10)),
  aux       = prior_spec("exponential", rate = 1 / 15)
)
priors
```

If you have no substantive knowledge to encode, leave components as `NULL`
to use rstanarm's autoscaled weakly informative defaults, or derive priors
from data with `empirical_bayes_priors()` (see the article on
*Data-informed priors*).

## 2. Check the priors before fitting

A prior predictive check simulates data from the priors alone. Test scores
cannot be negative, and scores above 200 would be absurd, so we declare
that range as plausible:

```{r}
pc <- prior_predictive_check(train, kid_score ~ mom_iq + mom_hs,
                             prior_config = priors,
                             plausible_range = c(0, 200), refresh = 0)
pc
plot(pc)
```

The simulated data sets are wider than the observed data, as weakly
informative priors should make them, but only
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * pc$summary$share_outside)` of simulated values fall
outside the plausible range.

## 3. Fit the model and verify the computation

```{r}
fit <- fit_model_with_prior(train, kid_score ~ mom_iq + mom_hs,
                            prior_config = priors,
                            chains = 4, iter = 1000, refresh = 0)
attr(fit, "bmb_convergence")
```

`fit_model_with_prior()` runs `check_convergence()` automatically with the
criteria of Vehtari et al. (2021): rank-normalised R-hat of at most 1.01,
bulk- and tail-ESS of at least 100 per chain, no divergent transitions and
E-BFMI of at least 0.3. If a check fails it warns and still returns the fit
so you can investigate. Rank plots show mixing problems more clearly than
trace plots:

```{r}
plot(attr(fit, "bmb_convergence"), type = "rank")
```

## 4. How much did the prior matter?

`plot_prior_posterior()` overlays each prior on its posterior:

```{r}
plot_prior_posterior(fit)
```

`prior_sensitivity()` quantifies the same question without refitting, by
power-scaling the prior and the likelihood (Kallioinen et al., 2023):

```{r}
sens <- prior_sensitivity(fit)
sens
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
flag_rows <- sens$summary[sens$summary$diagnosis != "-", ]
flagged <- paste0("\x60", flag_rows$variable, "\x60 (", flag_rows$diagnosis, ")", collapse = " and ")
conflict <- any(flag_rows$diagnosis == "prior-data conflict")
```

How to read the table:

* `contraction` near 1 means the data have sharpened the prior a lot.
* The `*_sens` columns measure how much the posterior mean and SD respond to
  strengthening the prior or the likelihood (0 = not at all).
* `conflict_z` measures disagreement between prior and data in standard-error
  units. A parameter whose prior is influential and whose `|conflict_z|` is
  2 or more is diagnosed as a prior-data conflict.

`r if (nrow(flag_rows) == 0) "No parameter is sensitive to the prior: the likelihood dominates, so the conclusions do not hinge on the exact priors chosen." else paste0("The diagnosis flags ", flagged, ": for each, \x60|prior_mean_sens|\x60 or \x60|prior_sd_sens|\x60 is at least 0.05. ", if (!conflict) "Every |conflict_z| is below 2, so prior and data agree." else "For a prior-data conflict, prior and data disagree, so revisit that prior.")`
The *Prior sensitivity* article shows what weakly informative, conflicting
and weakly identified cases look like.

## 5. Evaluate predictions

```{r}
perf <- evaluate_model_performance(fit, test)
perf
```

Besides RMSE and MAE of the posterior mean, bmbeR reports two proper
scoring rules, which also reward calibrated uncertainty: the held-out log
predictive density (ELPD) and the continuous ranked probability score
(CRPS). Coverage of the 90% predictive intervals close to 90% indicates
well-calibrated uncertainty.

## 6. Report

```{r}
report <- workflow_report(fit, prior_check = pc, sensitivity = sens,
                          performance = perf)
report
```

Items with status `check` need attention and `missing` items have not been
done yet; printed in the console, these show as `[check]` and `[ -- ]`. The
report computes posterior predictive p-values and PSIS-LOO cross-validation
from the fit itself, and runs `prior_sensitivity()` when no sensitivity
result is supplied.

## Where next

* *Choosing priors*: why scale matters, autoscaling, and prior predictive
  checks for logistic regression.
* *Data-informed priors*: unit-information, empirical Bayes and power priors,
  and why naively re-using the data is a mistake.
* *Convergence diagnostics*: what each criterion means and what failure looks like.
* *Prior sensitivity*: the theory behind the diagnostics, and refitting under
  alternative priors.
* *Predictive evaluation*: proper scoring rules and model comparison on held-out data.
